src.q: Atenolol 50 mg.
Atenolol 100 mg.

bnf.note: BNF/BNFC is only available in the UK; not accessed.

items.t: Hypertension; angina pectoris; cardiac arrhythmias; myocardial infarction (early intervention in the acute phase).

src.q: Management of hypertension. Management of angina pectoris. Management of cardiac arrhythmias. Management of myocardial infarction. Early intervention in the acute phase.

restrictions.note: No prescribing restriction stated in the UK atenolol 50 mg and 100 mg tablets SmPCs.

items.t: Adults: most respond to 100 mg once daily; some respond to 50 mg once daily. Full effect after 1-2 weeks. Use the lowest possible starting dose.

src.q: Most patients respond to 100 mg daily given orally as a single dose. Some patients, however, will respond to 50 mg given as a single daily dose.
The effect will be fully established after one to two weeks.
with the lowest possible starting dosage

items.t: Adults: 100 mg once daily or 50 mg twice daily. Higher doses are unlikely to add benefit.

src.q: Most patients with angina pectoris will respond to 100 mg given orally once daily or 50 mg given twice daily.
It is unlikely that additional benefit will be gained by increasing the dose.

items.t: Oral maintenance after arrhythmia control: 50-100 mg once daily.

src.q: a suitable oral maintenance dosage is 50-100 mg daily, given as a single dose.

items.t: Acute MI (within 12 hours, after IV atenolol): 50 mg orally about 15 minutes after the IV dose, 50 mg 12 hours later, then 100 mg once daily. Stop if bradycardia or hypotension needing treatment occurs.

src.q: followed by Tenormin 50 mg orally about 15 minutes later
This should be followed by a further 50 mg orally 12 hours after the intravenous dose, and then 12 hours later by 100 mg orally, once daily.
If bradycardia and/or hypotension requiring treatment, or any other untoward effects occur, Tenormin should be discontinued.

items.t: Elderly: dose needs may be lower, especially with impaired renal function; use with caution and start with a lower dose.

src.q: Dosage requirements may be reduced, especially in patients with impaired renal function.
Should be used with caution in the elderly, starting with a lesser dose

items.t: No paediatric experience; not recommended for use in children.

src.q: There is no paediatric experience with Tenormin and for this reason it is not recommended for use in children.

items.t: Hypersensitivity to atenolol or any excipient.

src.q: should not be used in patients with any of the following:
hypersensitivity to the active substance, or to any of the excipients listed in section 6.1

items.t: Cardiogenic shock; uncontrolled heart failure; sick sinus syndrome; second- or third-degree heart block.

src.q: should not be used in patients with any of the following:
cardiogenic shock uncontrolled heart failure sick sinus syndrome second-or third-degree heart block

items.t: Untreated phaeochromocytoma; metabolic acidosis; bradycardia (<45 bpm); hypotension; severe peripheral arterial circulatory disturbances.

src.q: should not be used in patients with any of the following:
untreated phaeochromocytoma metabolic acidosis bradycardia (<45 bpm) hypotension severe peripheral arterial circulatory disturbances.

items.t: Do not stop abruptly: withdraw gradually over 7-14 days, following patients during withdrawal (especially ischaemic heart disease).

src.q: Should not be withdrawn abruptly. The dosage should be withdrawn gradually over a period of 7-14 days
Patients should be followed during withdrawal, especially those with ischaemic heart disease.

items.t: Reversible obstructive airways disease (asthma): avoid unless there are compelling clinical reasons; then use with caution.

src.q: these should be avoided in patients with reversible obstructive airways disease, unless there are compelling clinical reasons for their use.
Where such reasons exist, Tenormin may be used with caution.

items.t: Controlled heart failure: may be used; caution if cardiac reserve is poor. First-degree heart block: caution.

src.q: may be used in patients whose signs of heart failure have been controlled. Caution must be exercised in patients whose cardiac reserve is poor.
caution must be exercised if it is given to patients with first-degree heart block.

items.t: Diabetes: may mask hypoglycaemia (especially tachycardia); with sulfonylureas the risk of severe hypoglycaemia may increase. Advise careful blood glucose monitoring.

src.q: May mask the symptoms of hypoglycaemia, in particular, tachycardia.
Beta-blockers could further increase the risk of severe hypoglycaemia when used concurrently with sulfonylureas.
Diabetic patients should be advised to carefully monitor blood glucose levels.

items.t: Prinzmetal's angina: may increase angina attacks; use only with utmost caution.

src.q: May increase the number and duration of angina attacks in patients with Prinzmetal's angina
its use may be considered although utmost caution must be exercised.

items.t: History of anaphylaxis: reactions to allergens may be more severe and may not respond to usual adrenaline doses.

src.q: May cause a more severe reaction to a variety of allergens when given to patients with a history of anaphylactic reaction to such allergens.
Such patients may be unresponsive to the usual doses of adrenaline (epinephrine) used to treat the allergic reactions.

items.t: Surgery: if stopping before surgery, stop at least 24 hours before; if continued, choose an anaesthetic with little negative inotropic activity.

src.q: this should be done at least 24 hours prior to the procedure.
If treatment is continued, an anaesthetic with little negative inotropic activity should be selected to minimise the risk of myocardial depression.

items.t: May mask signs of thyrotoxicosis; may aggravate less severe peripheral arterial disease; in phaeochromocytoma give an alpha-blocker as well.

src.q: May mask the signs of thyrotoxicosis.
may also aggravate less severe peripheral arterial circulatory disturbances.
in patients with a phaeochromocytoma, an alpha-blocker should be given concomitantly.

items.t: If symptomatic bradycardia with resting pulse below 50-55 bpm develops, reduce the dose.

src.q: the pulse rate drops to less than 50-55 bpm at rest, the dose should be reduced.

items.t: Verapamil or diltiazem (negative inotropic calcium-channel blockers): exaggerated effects possible, especially with impaired ventricular function or SA/AV conduction problems; may cause severe hypotension, bradycardia and cardiac failure. Do not give either one intravenously within 48 hours of stopping the other.

src.q: Combined use of beta-blockers and calcium channel blockers with negative inotropic effects, e.g. verapamil and diltiazem, can lead to an exaggeration of these effects
This may result in severe hypotension, bradycardia and cardiac failure.
Neither the beta-blocker nor the calcium channel blocker should be administered intravenously within 48 hours of discontinuing the other.

items.t: Dihydropyridines (e.g. nifedipine): increased risk of hypotension; cardiac failure may occur with latent cardiac insufficiency.

src.q: Concomitant therapy with dihydropyridines, e.g. nifedipine, may increase the risk of hypotension, and cardiac failure may occur in patients with latent cardiac insufficiency.

items.t: Insulin and oral antidiabetics: blood glucose lowering may be intensified; with sulfonylureas the risk of severe hypoglycaemia may increase; hypoglycaemia symptoms may be masked.

src.q: Concomitant use with insulin and oral antidiabetic drugs may lead to the intensification of the blood sugar lowering effects of these drugs.
The concomitant use of beta-blockers with sulfonylureas could increase the risk of severe hypoglycaemia.

items.t: NSAIDs (e.g. ibuprofen): may reduce the blood pressure lowering effect.

src.q: Concomitant use of prostaglandin synthetase-inhibiting drugs, e.g. ibuprofen and indometacin, may decrease the hypotensive effects of beta-blockers.

items.t: Sympathomimetics (e.g. adrenaline) may counteract beta-blockade.

src.q: Concomitant use of sympathomimetic agents, e.g. adrenaline (epinephrine), may counteract the effect of beta-blockers.

items.t: Clonidine: beta-blockers may worsen rebound hypertension; stop the beta-blocker several days before stopping clonidine. Digoxin, class I antiarrhythmics and amiodarone: additive conduction effects. Anaesthetics: choose an agent with little negative inotropic activity.

src.q: the beta-blocker should be withdrawn several days before discontinuing clonidine.
Digitalis glycosides, in association with beta-blockers, may increase atrioventricular conduction time.
Class I anti-arrhythmic drugs (e.g. disopyramide) and amiodarone may have a potentiating effect on atrial-conduction time and induce negative inotropic effect.

items.t: No significant accumulation if CrCl is above 35 ml/min/1.73 m2.

src.q: No significant accumulation of Tenormin occurs in patients who have a creatinine clearance greater than 35 ml/min/1.73 m2

items.t: CrCl 15-35 ml/min/1.73 m2: oral dose 50 mg daily.

src.q: For patients with a creatinine clearance of 15-35 ml/min/1.73 m2 (equivalent to serum creatinine of 300-600 micromol/litre), the oral dose should be 50 mg daily

items.t: CrCl below 15 ml/min/1.73 m2: oral dose 25 mg daily or 50 mg on alternate days.

src.q: For patients with a creatinine clearance of less than 15 ml/min/1.73 m2 (equivalent to serum creatinine of greater than 600 micromol/litre), the oral dose should be 25 mg daily or 50 mg on alternate days

items.t: Haemodialysis: 50 mg orally after each dialysis, under hospital supervision (marked falls in blood pressure can occur).

src.q: Patients on haemodialysis should be given 50 mg orally after each dialysis; this should be done under hospital supervision as marked falls in blood pressure can occur.

hepatic.note: No hepatic dose advice in the UK atenolol tablets SmPC (no significant hepatic metabolism stated in 5.2).

items.t: SmPC: use with caution. Crosses the placenta; associated with intra-uterine growth retardation; weigh benefit against risk, particularly in the first and second trimesters.

src.q: Caution should be exercised when Tenormin is administered during pregnancy or to a woman who is breast-feeding.
Administration of Tenormin to pregnant women in the management of mild to moderate hypertension has been associated with intra-uterine growth retardation.
requires that the anticipated benefit be weighed against the possible risks, particularly in the first and second trimesters

items.t: BUMPS: can be used in pregnancy if recommended by a doctor; no concern about birth defects; babies may be smaller; extra growth scans may be offered at around 32 and 36 weeks.

src.q: Atenolol can be used in pregnancy if recommended by a doctor.
There are no concerns that beta blockers cause birth defects, stillbirth or preterm birth.
Women taking atenolol may be more likely to have a smaller baby.
you may be offered extra scans at around 32 and 36 weeks to check the growth of your baby.

items.t: SmPC: use with caution. Significant accumulation in breast milk; breastfed neonates may be at risk of hypoglycaemia and bradycardia.

src.q: There is significant accumulation of Tenormin in breast milk.
Neonates born to mothers who are receiving Tenormin at parturition or breast-feeding may be at risk of hypoglycaemia and bradycardia.

items.t: SPS: use with caution; labetalol, metoprolol or propranolol are preferred. Monitor the infant for bradycardia or hypoglycaemia (drowsiness, lethargy, poor feeding, poor weight gain); risk of accumulation, especially in neonates.

src.q: It can be used with caution during breastfeeding, but labetalol, metoprolol, or propranolol are preferred if clinically appropriate..
There is therefore significant risk of accumulation of atenolol in breastfed infants, particularly neonates, resulting in increased risk of adverse effects.

reproductive.note: No fertility or contraception advice in the UK atenolol tablets SmPC. BUMPS: no increased risk expected if the father takes atenolol.

items.t: Rare: worsening heart failure, heart block, bronchospasm in asthma, hepatic toxicity (intrahepatic cholestasis), thrombocytopenia/purpura. Not known: angioedema, urticaria, lupus-like syndrome.

src.q: Rare Heart failure deterioration, precipitation of heart block
Rare Bronchospasm may occur in patients with bronchial asthma or a history of asthmatic complaints
Rare Hepatic toxicity including intrahepatic cholestasis
Rare Purpura, thrombocytopenia
Not known Hypersensitivity reactions, including angioedema and urticaria

src.q: The symptoms of overdosage may include bradycardia, hypotension, acute cardiac insufficiency and bronchospasm.
